1:
Delitzsch points out what is singular here: it is the only psalm titled tehillah, whose plural became the collective name of the whole book. The Talmud's promise that whoever repeats it three times a day may be sure of the world to come he sets out and explains — not because it runs the alphabet, since Psalm 119 does that eightfold, nor because it celebrates God's care for every creature, since the Great Hallel does too, but because this psalm unites both. Clarke and Calvin report the same rabbinic saying independently. Clarke, finding no occasion for the psalm unless simple gratitude, notes that the Hebrew and all the versions give it to David; Calvin passes on Morison's guess that David wrote it when Israel received what the psalm before had asked, and that this is the new song he there promised.

Augustine reads the title christologically: praise to David himself means praise to Christ, who came of the seed of David and yet, in his divine nature, is David's Creator and Lord. From that he draws an argument about timing: begin praising now if you intend to praise for ever, since whoever will not praise in this transitory age will be silent when age upon age has come. Bless him every day, so that when the single days have passed and the day without end has come, you may go from praise to praise as from strength to strength. It is no wonder to bless God on a day of joy; the question is the day of sorrow.

Henry makes the same point domestically. Praising God must be daily work, and no day may pass without it, however busy or sorrowful; it is the most needful of our daily employments and the most delightful of our comforts, and since God is every day doing well for us we should every day speak well of him. He hears three things in for ever and ever: that David meant to continue to the end of his life, that his psalms should serve the church to the end of time, and that he expected to praise God through eternity — those whose constant work on earth is praise having it as their everlasting bliss in heaven. He notices too that praise is not confined to solemn devotion but belongs in ordinary conversation, no subject being more noble, copious, pleasant, useful and unexceptionable than the glory of God.

Spurgeon sets the two kingships side by side: David, being God's king, adores God as his king, and it is well when the Lord's royalty arouses our loyalty. Praise, he says, is for all tenses; where a man cannot express all his praise now it is wise to register the resolution as a bond. Our praise of God shall be as eternal as the God we praise. Calvin draws a political point from the same verse. The psalm was probably written when David's kingdom was flourishing, so it is worth noticing that in calling God his King he puts himself and every earthly prince in place, letting no distinction interfere with the glory due to God. Gill takes the King for the Messiah throughout, and insists this great King is no creature but God.

The third verse defeats them all, which is the point. Clarke renders it that to his mightinesses there is no investigation, all in God being unlimited; Ellicott gives the more expressive literal form, and for his greatness no search. Calvin turns the unmeasurableness into a rule: we praise God aright only when filled and overwhelmed with ecstatic admiration of the immensity of his power, and that admiration is the fountain from which our praises proceed according to our capacity. Ellicott says that in contemplating such greatness time ceases to be. Clarke reaches for Addison: through all eternity a joyful song I'll raise, but O, eternity's too short to utter all thy praise.
4:
Transmission is the subject of verse 4, and Clarke draws a line. God's creating and redeeming acts are recorded in his word, but his providential dealings must be handed down by tradition, being in continual occurrence and therefore innumerable. Ellicott catches the same open-endedness in the grammar: the verb is better rendered praises, with the idea of indefinite continuance, and so through the following verses. He tidies two other words on the way: the speaking of verse 5 may be singing, the verb being often rendered meditate, and what is spoken of is not wondrous works so much as the details of the wonders, of which psalms like the hundred and fifth are the fulfilment. The uttering of verse 7 means literally to pour forth in a stream.

What the terrible acts of verse 6 are Gill answers christologically, as he does the psalm throughout. He counts the flood, the fire on Sodom, and the works in Egypt and at the Red Sea, which the saints of the former dispensation could speak of; then the acts at the cross, where the serpent's head was bruised and the principalities destroyed, the sun darkened at noon, the earth quaked, the rocks split and the veil torn, so that the centurion and his guard were thrown into a panic. Ellicott's note there is one point of text: the written form gives greatnesses in the plural, as Aquila and Jerome read it, and the parallelism decidedly favours it.

Verse 8 gathers the old self-description of God, and Delitzsch marks that the writer took it over as the hundred and third psalm did, with one change: not abundant in mercy but great in mercy. God's real will, he says, tends towards the favour that gladly stoops to give and the compassion that interests itself on another's behalf. Spurgeon works the same clause negatively: nothing in Jehovah is suspicious, prejudiced, morose, tyrannical or unapproachable, and if he is full of compassion there is no room in him for forgetfulness or harshness. What an ocean of compassion there must be, he adds, since the infinite God is full of it. Even those who refuse the grace still share the long-suffering.

Then verse 9, where the two readings collide. Gill will not take the Lord is good to all as providential goodness to all creatures; it is the special goodness of Christ, reaching all the chosen — Gentile as well as Jew, since he tasted death for them and the gospel has been sent to both — which is why he thinks the psalm belongs to gospel times, the grace of Christ appearing larger in it. Clarke reads the same words the opposite way, and with heat. There is not a soul out of hell that is not continually under God's most merciful regards, so far is he from decreeing before their creation the damnation of any man; his bowels of compassion are over all his works, and he feels for his intelligent offspring as the most affectionate mother for the child of her own bosom. Through that mercy his son tasted death for every man. How far, Clarke asks, is all that is here spoken of the nature of God from the Molochian doctrine of the eternal decree of reprobation — and he sets a verse against it: his grace for every soul is free, for his who forged the dire decree, for every reprobate and me.

Gill had already measured that goodness at verse 7, making it great three ways: in its spring, good will and free favour and not the works or merits of men; in the multitude it reaches, a number no man can number out of every nation; and in the benefits bestowed through it. He adds that the remembering is itself assisted, the Spirit bringing the goodness to mind, and that under the gospel an ordinance was appointed to refresh the memory.
10:
Henry draws the distinction the tenth verse asks for. All God's works praise him, but only his saints bless him: the works praise him as a building praises its builder or a well-drawn picture its painter, while the saints bless him as the children of tender parents rise up and call them blessed. The works praise him objectively; the saints praise him actively, collecting the rent of praise from the inferior creatures and paying it into the treasury above. Clarke reads the same word for saints as the compassionate ones, who have partaken of the great mercy of verse 8, and says they bless God because they know and feel that he wills the salvation of all — unlike the dark, the gloomy, the hard-hearted, the narrow-minded bigots who never had that love shed abroad in their hearts and can unfeelingly deal in the damnation of their fellows. Gill keeps his line, taking the works that praise God for the workmanship of his grace.

On the kingdom they reach for comparisons and withdraw them. Henry offers the courts of Solomon and Ahasuerus, then says that beside the glorious majesty of God's kingdom they were but glow-worms to the sun. Spurgeon remembers a palace dedicated to all the glories of France, and answers that time, eternity and all space are filled with the glories of God. He presses the power further than the glory: all power comes from God, and apart from him the laws of nature would be inoperative, so he is the one source of force, mechanical, vital, mental and spiritual. Beyond the power already put forth, infinite force lies latent in him. Who can calculate the reserve forces of the Infinite — and how then can his kingdom fail? Gill locates the kingdom carefully: not only that of nature and providence which rules over all, but rather the kingdom of grace, not worldly but spiritual, coming not with outward observation but lying within the heart.

Perpetuity is the point of verse 13, and Henry states it as contrast: the thrones of earthly princes totter, the flowers of their crowns wither and monarchies end, but this kingdom is everlasting, because God is eternal and his counsels unchangeable. Gill sets it against the Babylonian, Persian, Grecian and Roman monarchies, all of which have had or will have an end, and offers a second rendering — a kingdom of all worlds, or of all ages — reaching to heaven, earth and hell, and to all times.

And then the psalm loses a letter. It is the last of the acrostics, and the stanza that should open with nun is missing from the Hebrew. Clarke will not accept that it never existed, since the alphabet is incomplete without it, and calls its loss an unanswerable argument for the careless manner in which the Jews preserved the divine records. He prints the line the Syriac, Greek, Latin and Anglo-Saxon all carry — the Lord is faithful in all his words, and merciful in all his works — and notes that a manuscript in Trinity College, Dublin has it in Hebrew at the foot of the page, though he supposes it was put there by correction.

Ellicott agrees the stanza has most probably dropped away, then argues against the supplement on every ground he can find: it is only a variation of verse 17, unknown to the other ancient versions, rejected by the Jewish writers, and suspicious in the single Hebrew manuscript that has it. Having said all that, he concedes the arguments can hardly weigh against the improbability that in so artificial a composition one letter — an easy one at that — should have been left out of the draft; nor against the further improbability that the Greek translators would trouble to supply a verse to keep up an alphabetical arrangement of which they took no other notice, and perhaps hardly observed.
14:
Ellicott thinks verse 14 a turn in the history of religion: a grand step in theology, he says, when the first instance of divine majesty is sought in God's condescension to human weakness and pity for frailty and want. The heathen had seen that this was king-like — he quotes Ovid, that to succour the fallen is, believe me, a royal thing — but had hardly seen it was also god-like. Spurgeon puts the same contrast against the verse before: he who reigns in glorious majesty stoops to lift up those apt to fall. The form of the verb tells him it is continuous, so that God is Jehovah upholding; and he presses on the choice of object. The fallen of our race are shunned by us — fallen women especially, he says — and it is peculiar tenderness in the Lord that these are whom he looks upon. The Lord loves to reverse things: he puts down the lofty and lifts up the lowly.

Clarke takes the word as the falling, those unable to keep their feet, and calls God their prop, adding that no man falls through his own weakness merely: if he rely on God the strongest foe cannot shake him. Gill, as everywhere here, narrows the reference: not all who fell in Adam, nor all who fall into sin, but the subjects of Christ's kingdom — and he passes on Aben Ezra's point that no mortal king does this, since an earthly king raises one man and depresses another.

The next two verses are where the two readings pull hardest. Clarke sees the whole animal creation looking up as the young of every species look to their parents for food, God being the universal Father who provides for every living thing, in the food suited to each and every stage of life. He calls it a wonderful mystery that all are so provided for, that all expect it and not one is disappointed. What a hand it is that holds all the food meeting the desires of the universe of creatures. Wesley agrees, adding that expectation is figuratively ascribed to brute creatures. Gill will have none of it: the eyes are not those of the beasts of the field or fish of the sea but of the Lord's people, who look for spiritual food as well as bread; and the hand opened is not of providence but of grace.

On the righteousness of verse 17 Spurgeon includes the work most likely to be doubted. Whatever God does must be right, and in saving his people he is as righteous and holy as in anything else: he has not shown mercy at the expense of justice, but magnified his righteousness by the death of his Son. Clarke, still worrying at the missing letter, suggests this verse's resemblance to the lost one caused the loss.

Nearness closes the psalm. Spurgeon distinguishes two kinds: God is near not merely by omnipresence but to sympathise and favour, and not for a few who invoke him but for every one of the company — in truth being added because many formal prayers and false professions never bring a man into communion. Ellicott's whole note is Tennyson's line, that God is closer than breathing, nearer than hands and feet. At the end Clarke finds his etymology and his theology in one pair of syllables: the guardian of the pious and the destroyer of the wicked are two words a single letter apart, the first implying that he keeps them continually, the second that the others are destroyed. Ellicott notes the same recurrence more coolly, that guardianship of the good implies destruction of the wicked; and Clarke turns the pair into a last invitation: as near as one word is to the other, so near is God a Saviour to those standing on the brink of destruction, if they will look to him.
